one_liner: Single-file C++20 database buffer manager that uses virtual memory for page translation; beats mmap-based LMDB and WiredTiger on TPC-C.
what_it_does: vmcache is the SIGMOD'23 research buffer manager: it reserves a large anonymous virtual region the size of the storage device, keeps a per-page state word (version plus Unlocked/shared/Locked/Marked/Evicted), and reads or writes 4KB pages explicitly with O_DIRECT pread and libaio, so the database controls caching and eviction rather than the kernel page cache. It ships with a B-tree and TPC-C and random-lookup drivers configured by environment variables (BLOCK, VIRTGB, PHYSGB, EXMAP, THREADS, DATASIZE). It is a benchmarkable engine, not a library with a stable API; reuse means lifting the BufferManager/PageState code from vmcache.cpp.
how_it_is_fast: Page IDs map straight to virtual addresses, so hot-path page access needs no hash-table lookup or pointer swizzling; correctness comes from optimistic version-validated latches in a 64-bit atomic state word per page. Eviction is a clock over a lock-free resident-page hash set and drops frames in batches (BATCH, default 64) with madvise(MADV_DONTNEED). With the optional exmap kernel module, page allocation and freeing go through per-thread ioctl batches on a VMA the kernel does not manage, which avoids Linux's TLB-shootdown and page-table locking bottlenecks during eviction.
when_to_use: Building or studying a storage engine whose working set exceeds RAM on fast NVMe, where you want mmap-like pointer access without mmap's uncontrolled eviction and write-back
In-memory or mostly-cached OLTP workloads: the paper (snippet) reports almost 90 M lookups/s and about 3 M TPC-C transactions/s with a 128 GB pool
Out-of-memory random reads on Linux where you can load a kernel module: exmap adds about 60% over plain vmcache by sidestepping kernel eviction scalability limits (snippet)
As an MIT-licensed reference for optimistic latching and virtual-memory-based page translation to port into your own engine
when_not_to_use: Out-of-memory random lookups where peak steady-state throughput matters: the paper snippet says vmcache is substantially slower than LeanStore there because it is bound by the kernel
Workloads that delete data: storage free-space management is an open TODO and allocCount only grows, so pages are never reused on disk
Environments where you cannot set vm.overcommit_memory=1 or load kernel modules (exmap uses a kallsyms workaround for non-exported symbols and has no LICENSE file)
Heavy lock contention: latches spin; C++ wait/notify is listed as a TODO
Non-Linux platforms: depends on Linux mmap/madvise semantics, libaio and O_DIRECT

integration.dependencies: libaio; optional exmap kernel module (tuhhosg/exmap, MODULE_LICENSE GPL, no LICENSE file)
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 (tested by the authors); needs a block device or file opened with O_DIRECT
integration.thread_safety: Multi-threaded by design (up to 128 worker threads, maxWorkerThreads), optimistic and exclusive page latches; each thread needs a workerThreadId

gotchas: VIRTGB must be at least the device size and larger values need vm.overcommit_memory=1; running out of virtual pages exits with 'VIRTGB is too low'
Page size is a compile-time 4096; issue #1 reports that switching to 2MB pages made the B-tree allocate far too many pages (closed without a documented fix)
Built with -fnon-call-exceptions because optimistic reads can touch evicted pages and restart via exceptions; keep those flags if you vendor the code
Default BLOCK is /tmp/bm, a regular file, so default runs do not measure a raw NVMe device
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick vmcache over UMap or FastMap when you are writing a DBMS and want the engine, not the kernel, to decide eviction and I/O, with an MIT license; pick TriCache or UMap when you need to accelerate an unmodified mmap-based application instead of rewriting its storage layer.
verified_claims_summary: The SIGMOD'23 paper (snippets only; the TUM, TUHH, TU Braunschweig and ACM copies are egress-blocked here) compares vmcache and vmcache+exmap with LeanStore, WiredTiger and mmap-based LMDB on TPC-C and random lookups: in memory vmcache reaches almost 90 M lookups/s and about 3 M TPC-C txn/s, WiredTiger trails significantly and LMDB does not scale on TPC-C, and out of memory exmap adds about 60% on random lookups, though LeanStore stays faster there. The repo has the driver and the Makefile flags but no results, hardware or CPU model.
status_note: Research code with recent commits (2025-09-09) and an MIT license; small enough (one 1,855-line vmcache.cpp plus TPC-C headers) to vendor, but missing storage free-space management.
sources_read: WebSearch: Virtual-Memory Assisted Buffer Management evaluation (snippets of the paper)
